title: Castle on the Grid
directAnswer: A move slides the piece in one direction across any number of empty cells until a wall ('X') or the border stops it — every cell passed over in that slide is reachable in the same single move. Minimize moves with BFS where each pop expands all four directions over their full open run, assigning distance + 1 to newly reached cells. Stop the slide at a wall/edge, or prune it once it reaches a cell already discovered at an earlier-or-equal BFS level. O(N²) cells, near O(N²) with pruning.

remember.pattern: BFS where each move expands a full row/column run
rules: **One move = a full slide**: every empty cell between the start and the stopping wall/edge costs the *same* single move.
BFS (not DFS) gives the minimum because all cells at distance d are settled before any at d + 1.
**Keep walking past same-level cells** (distance == d + 1): they were reached via a different direction and may not have swept this line yet.
**Prune** a slide only when it hits a cell with distance ≤ current d — that cell already sweeps the rest of the line.
Stop a slide at the **border or an 'X'**; the cell holding the 'X' is not enterable.
whenToUse: Shortest path on a grid where a 'move' covers a **variable distance** in a straight line
Unweighted in the sense that every slide costs exactly 1 → BFS
You need the minimum number of moves, not the exact cells traversed
antiSignals: Each step costs the cell-to-cell distance (weighted) → Dijkstra/0-1 BFS, not plain BFS
Moves are single-cell only → standard 4-neighbor grid BFS
Diagonal or knight moves → different neighbor generation
You must output the path of cells → store parent pointers, not just distances
remember.takeaway: Castle on the Grid is BFS with a non-standard neighbor rule: a node's neighbors are *all* cells reachable in one straight slide, not just the four adjacent cells. Once you redefine 'neighbor' as 'every cell in the open run', the classic unweighted-shortest-path BFS solves it unchanged.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you model a 'slide until blocked' move as BFS over full-row/column neighbors (constant cost per slide), rather than weighting by distance, and handle walls, borders, and revisits correctly.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Adding the slide length to the cost (turning it into a weighted problem), stopping a slide at the first already-visited cell unconditionally (which can overestimate), or using DFS and losing the shortest-path guarantee.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Frame it as 'redefine neighbors as the whole open run, then it's vanilla unweighted BFS', and justify the pruning rule precisely — you may only stop a slide at a cell discovered at an earlier-or-equal level, never at a same-next-level cell.

problemStatement:
You are given an `N × N` grid where each cell is `.` (open) or `X` (blocked), plus a start position `(startRow, startCol)` and a goal `(goalRow, goalCol)`. A **move** picks one of the four directions (up, down, left, right) and slides the piece across consecutive open cells until it is stopped by the grid border or a blocked cell — you may stop at any open cell along that line, and the entire slide counts as **one move**.

Return the **minimum number of moves** to get from the start to the goal.
constraints: Start and goal are open cells; they may coincide (answer 0)
Coordinates are 0-indexed: (row, col), row downward, col rightward
A path from start to goal always exists for the given inputs
understanding: The piece moves like a rook: in one move it travels in a straight line over any number of open cells until a wall or the border halts it. So the cost is the number of *slides*, not the number of cells crossed — a long straight glide is as cheap as a single step. That makes every slide an edge of weight 1, so the minimum number of moves is an unweighted shortest path, solvable by BFS. The only twist versus textbook grid BFS is neighbor generation: instead of the four adjacent cells, a cell's neighbors are *all* cells reachable along its four open runs.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does a move cost the number of cells slid, or just one?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just one. Sliding across five open cells is a single move, which is why this is unweighted BFS rather than Dijkstra.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I stop partway along a slide?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — you may stop at any open cell on the line, so every cell along the run is reachable in that one move.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What stops a slide?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The grid border or a blocked 'X' cell. You can never enter or pass through an 'X'.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if start equals goal?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Zero moves — the BFS returns the start's distance of 0 immediately.

approaches.name: Re-Expanding BFS (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: State the straightforward version first: BFS where each pop slides all four directions over their full open run, enqueuing newly reached cells but walking past already-visited ones to the wall.
hints: Each move costs 1 regardless of slide length, so this is an unweighted shortest path — what algorithm gives minimum unweighted distance?
BFS. The only change from textbook grid BFS is the neighbor rule: from a cell, slide in each of the four directions and treat every open cell on the run as a neighbor at distance + 1.
Walk each direction to the wall/border, assigning distance to unvisited cells. Continuing past visited cells re-walks lines, but it's simple and correct — O(N³).
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are N² cells; each is dequeued once. From each, the four slides can traverse up to N cells, and the baseline keeps walking even past already-visited cells, so a single pop costs O(N). Total O(N² · N) = O(N³). With N ≤ 100 that's ~10⁶ — fast enough, but it re-scans the same lines repeatedly.
approaches.explanation:
Recognizing the constant cost per slide reduces the problem to unweighted BFS; the implementation just needs the right neighbor rule.

**Setup.** A `dist` matrix initialized to -1 (unvisited); set `dist[start] = 0` and enqueue the start. BFS pops cells in nondecreasing distance order.

**Neighbor generation.** For a popped cell `(r, c)`, take each of the four direction vectors. Walk step by step: while the next cell is in bounds and not an `X`, it is reachable in one more move. If it's unvisited, set its distance to `dist[r][c] + 1` and enqueue it. Then keep stepping in the same direction until a wall or the border stops the slide.

**Why it's correct.** Every slide is an edge of weight 1, and BFS settles all distance-`d` cells before any distance-`(d+1)` cell, so the first time a cell is assigned a distance, that distance is minimal. Returning `dist[goal]` (or detecting the goal on pop) yields the fewest moves.

**Why we don't ship it as-is.** The baseline re-walks each line every time any cell on it is processed, because it strides past already-visited cells to the wall. That redundant scanning is the O(N³) cost the optimized version trims with a pruning rule.
approaches.insight: The whole problem is 'unweighted BFS with a custom neighbor function'. Once neighbors are defined as 'every cell in the open run', no special distance math is needed — the count of BFS layers is the answer.

approaches.name: BFS with Slide Pruning (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The refined version. Phrase it as 'same BFS, but cut a slide short once it reaches a cell already discovered at an earlier-or-equal level, since that cell already sweeps the rest of the line'.
hints: The baseline re-walks each line many times. When sliding and you reach a cell already reached at distance ≤ the current cell's distance, what does that tell you about the cells beyond it?
That cell was (or will be) processed no later than now, and when processed it sweeps the same line — so the cells beyond it are already covered optimally. You can stop the slide there.
But do NOT stop at a cell whose distance equals current + 1: it was reached from a perpendicular direction and may not have swept this line yet, so keep walking past it.
approaches.complexityReasoning: With the pruning rule, each grid line is fully swept only by the earliest BFS level that touches it; later slides into it stop immediately. Each of the N² cells is assigned once, and the total sweeping work amortizes to O(N²). Space is the O(N²) distance grid and queue.
approaches.explanation:
The correctness of BFS is untouched; the optimization removes redundant re-walking by reasoning about when a line is already fully covered.

**The pruning rule.** Suppose we pop cell `u` at distance `d` and slide in some direction, reaching cell `v` with recorded distance `dv`:
- If `v` is **unvisited** (`-1`): assign `d + 1`, enqueue, and continue the slide.
- If `dv ≤ d`: `v` was discovered at an earlier-or-equal BFS level, so it has been or will be processed by the time level `d` finishes, and its own slide in this direction sweeps every cell beyond it — assigning them `dv + 1 ≤ d + 1`, which is no worse than what `u` would give. So the rest of the line is already optimal; **break**.
- If `dv = d + 1`: `v` was reached this level from a *perpendicular* slide and has not yet swept this line. Beyond `v` there may be cells that only `u`'s slide reaches at `d + 1` (via `v` they'd cost `d + 2`). So **do not break** — keep walking, just don't reassign `v`.

**Why the `dv = d + 1` distinction matters.** Naively breaking at the first visited cell is a classic bug: it can leave cells beyond a same-level cell to be reached one move too late, overestimating the answer. The safe rule breaks only when the encountered cell is from a strictly-or-equally-earlier layer.

**Result.** Every line gets fully swept exactly once — by the earliest layer that enters it — collapsing the work to O(N²). The BFS layering still guarantees the first distance assigned to each cell (and to the goal) is the minimum number of moves.
approaches.insight: The subtlety isn't the BFS — it's knowing exactly when a slide is redundant. A cell already reached at an earlier-or-equal level dominates the rest of its line; a same-next-level cell does not. Encoding that precisely turns an O(N³) re-scan into an O(N²) sweep without sacrificing correctness.

pitfalls: Breaking the slide at the first visited cell unconditionally — overestimates when that cell is at distance d + 1.
Treating slide length as cost — use Dijkstra only if the problem actually weights by distance.
Off-by-one in bounds or reading grid[nr][nc] before the bounds check.
Returning before the goal is dequeued when distances on enqueue would also work — both are fine, but be consistent.

commonMistakes: Counting cells crossed as cost instead of one move per slide.
Using DFS, which doesn't yield the minimum number of moves.
Stopping a slide at any visited cell, including same-next-level cells, causing overestimates.
Failing to stop the slide at the border or an 'X'.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Weighting by slide length
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Each slide is one move no matter how far it travels. Adding the number of cells crossed makes it a weighted problem and yields the wrong minimum.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: dist[nr][nc] = dist[r][c] + steps   # steps = cells slid — wrong cost model
commonMistakesDetailed.good: dist[nr][nc] = dist[r][c] + 1       # one move per slide

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Unconditional break on visited
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Breaking at the first already-visited cell is unsafe when that cell sits at distance d + 1 (reached perpendicularly): cells beyond it may only be reachable at d + 1 through this slide, so stopping records them as d + 2.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: if (dist[nr][nc] != -1) break;   // breaks even on same-next-level cells
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if (dist[nr][nc] == -1) { dist[nr][nc] = d + 1; queue.offer(...); }
else if (dist[nr][nc] <= d) break;   // only earlier/equal levels

commonMistakesDetailed.title: DFS instead of BFS
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Move minimization is an unweighted shortest path; DFS explores deeply and can settle a cell with a non-minimal move count, returning a wrong answer.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: stack = [(start_row, start_col)]   # LIFO → depth-first, not shortest
commonMistakesDetailed.good: queue = deque([(start_row, start_col)])   # FIFO → BFS, shortest first

patternNote: Canonical Unweighted BFS with a Custom Neighbor Rule. Recognize it when a single 'move' covers a variable straight-line distance: redefine a cell's neighbors as every cell in its open run, then run plain BFS. The pruning insight — stop a slide only at cells discovered at an earlier-or-equal level — drops the re-scan from O(N³) to O(N²) without affecting correctness.
